title: Fast fashion and who actually changes

turns.speaker: Divya
turns.text: The figure that stopped me was that the average garment now gets worn about seven times before it's thrown away.

turns.speaker: Cara
turns.text: And the price makes it rational. If a top costs four pounds, repairing it is irrational, and so is caring about it.

turns.speaker: Divya
turns.text: The usual answer is buy better, buy less, which works fine if you can spend eighty pounds on a coat.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Right, and that's where the moralising falls apart. It's cheap to be told to buy expensive things.

turns.speaker: Cara
turns.text: Although the second-hand market genuinely has changed, and that isn't a rich person's option.

turns.speaker: Divya
turns.text: It's changed for the resellable end. Nobody's reselling a four-pound top, they're binning it.

turns.speaker: Divya
turns.text: So second hand thrives on exactly the clothes that weren't the problem.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: That's a good point. The charity shops are drowning in the cheap stuff.

turns.speaker: Cara
turns.text: Where it does shift is when the cost lands on the producer. France put a levy on each item and it moved the numbers more than a decade of campaigns did.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Because a company responds to a price and a person responds to a mood.

turns.speaker: Divya
turns.text: I'd put it less cynically, but yes.

turns.speaker: Cara
turns.text: The uncomfortable part is that this industry employs millions of people who need it to keep selling.

points: The average garment is worn about seven times before disposal.
Cara argues very low prices make repair and attachment irrational.
Divya and Nate reject the advice to buy better and buy less as unaffordable for many.
Divya argues second-hand markets only work for resellable clothing, not the cheapest items, which are binned and overwhelm charity shops.
Cara cites a French levy on each item as more effective than a decade of consumer campaigns, because firms respond to prices.
Cara notes the unresolved difficulty that millions of jobs depend on the industry continuing to sell.
